questions.q: What is the one mechanical task every LLM is actually trained to perform?
options: Predicting a probability distribution over what token comes next, given the sequence so far
Looking up answers in a fixed database
Translating every input into a single universal language first
Running a search engine query before responding
questions.explain: Underneath everything an LLM appears to do, the core mechanism is always the same: compute a probability for every possible next token given the text so far.

options: Randomly picking any token regardless of probability
Always picking the single highest-probability token
Picking the longest available token
Ignoring the probability distribution entirely
questions.explain: Greedy decoding always selects the single most probable next token, which is deterministic but can produce repetitive text.

questions.q: What does "autoregressive" mean in the context of LLM generation?
options: Each new token is generated based on all tokens that came before it, including ones the model just produced
The model regresses to an earlier, simpler version of itself
Generation happens for the entire response at once, in a single step
The model automatically corrects earlier mistakes before continuing
questions.explain: Autoregressive generation means each token is predicted based on the full sequence so far — including the model's own previously generated tokens — one token at a time.

questions.q: Why does generating a longer response typically take more time?
options: Longer responses are always generated in a single step, which is slower
The model switches to a different, slower algorithm for long text
Every new token requires a fresh pass over the entire sequence generated so far
Longer responses require downloading more data from the internet
questions.explain: Because generation is autoregressive, each new token means re-processing the whole sequence so far — so more tokens means more total passes.

questions.q: What do top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling have in common?
options: Both always pick the lowest-probability token
Both restrict random sampling to a subset of the most plausible candidate tokens
Both disable randomness entirely, like greedy decoding
Both are only used during model training, never during generation
questions.explain: Top-k and top-p both narrow the pool of candidate tokens to the most plausible ones before sampling, avoiding wildly implausible choices while still allowing some randomness.
